The post The Road to Great Wine With Eben Sadie appeared first on Vinography.
content:
When one of the world’s most talented and ambitious winemakers decides to lay out what sounds like a grand unified field theory for making great wine, you shut your mouth and listen. Last autumn, I had the good fortune to spend an afternoon with Eben Sadie at his estate in the Swartland region of South Africa. We were joined by a small group of buyers from Madagascar, who were meeting Sadie for the first time.

Perhaps because these were new acquaintances, and perhaps because of these visitors’ unfamiliarity with his wines and with the region, Sadie offered them an unusually in-depth introduction.

Sitting in the lounge of his new winery, along with his elder son Markus, he launched into a narrative that was by far the most comprehensive articulation of his personal history and winemaking philosophy that I’ve ever heard. I managed to record it, and have decided to offer the transcript of it here in its entirety, only lightly edited for readability.

What he had to say seemed to hang together as a single, relatively linear narrative, and it felt to me as though it was worthy of an extended read. I hope you will feel the same way.

In a recent interview with Jancis Robinson, Sadie announced that 2027 will be his last as the winemaker for his family estate, The Sadie Family Wines. He is handing the reins to his son Markus and his daughter-in-law Jessica. Sadie says he plans to continue his research and work in the vineyards, but will leave the work in the cellar to the kids.

Those who want to just skip to my thoughts on the spectacular wines of Sadie’s most recent vintage can jump to the reviews here.

Otherwise, here’s Eben Sadie explaining, well, everything.

I did not grow up in a family of wine. I grew up on the coast here in the Swartland, completely disconnected from wine and food. We ate food because we wanted to stay alive, but we didn’t know that food could be something else. I grew up in a pretty small village. Nobody was rich, nobody was really very poor. It was just balanced—everybody living in each other’s houses—that kind of life.

I grew up loving the ocean a lot. I mean, you love living in a beautiful place where the ocean is very much a part of your life. I was always windsurfing, kitesurfing, surfing, diving. There was a point in my life when I thought I would study Marine Biology.

So for me, ultimately, it was between Marine Biology and Agriculture. In 1990, at that time, you still had to go to the military in South Africa; it was compulsory. So I went to the military in 1990. And by the time I had almost finished with the military, I decided I would study agriculture.

I went to go study in Stellenbosch. And when you study agriculture in Stellenbosch, you are almost never disconnected from wine. Stellenbosch is such a genius town, you know. In Stellenbosch, everything is wine. And from living there and studying there, my contact with wine grew more and more.

As a young student, I joined a tasting group, and I started tasting the great wines. There was a very important restaurant there at the time, run by Mark Kent, that today is Boekenhoutskloof. Mark introduced me to a lot of the great wines of the world at that early stage. I was 20 years old when I tasted Latour, Mouton, Haut-Brion, Cheval Blanc, Ausone—all those wines. And for me, it changed my world. 

Studying, we didn’t always have the money to taste wines, but we found ways. I chose to work in restaurants. It was one way to finance my drinking. My life was work in restaurants, get money, buy wine, drink wine. So by the time I was going into my third year at Stellenbosch, I decided to study oenology. But I came into wine through drinking, not studying.

I was drinking wine and saying to myself, I want to do this.

It’s important to know that when I qualified [from university] it was 1994. That’s a very important date, because it’s also the year of the birth of the new South Africa. I was finalizing my studies at the same time the new South Africa was being born. So when I started my career, I started my career in the New South Africa, not the Old South Africa. It’s an important point because in a way, I’m the oldest qualified ‘young’ winemaker in the New South Africa. 

Had I qualified two years before, I would not have had the same entry into the world. When I finished studying, I could all of a sudden go anywhere in the world. Before that, we were embargoed. We couldn’t travel. And that is very important.

Many of the winemakers who are my senior, all our senior winemakers—my mentors—they couldn’t travel. And that’s a big difference. I believe that in life, if you want to become the best, you have to work with the best.

If I want to compete in the Tour de France, if I want to ride with those guys, I cannot just ride my bicycle around here. I have to go ride with them. If I want to run like Usain Bolt, I have to pack my bags, I have to go to Jamaica, and I have to start running with him every day. When he wakes up, I wake up. If he puts on his shoes, I put on my shoes. I start running when he starts running, and I stop running only when he stops running. Or I run more. There’s no way to become the top in the world if you don’t play with the top. There’s no other way. You need the time. You need the contact. You need to learn about determination, tenacity, ambition, drive, all those things.

You cannot learn those just looking at your neighbor here. Nothing will happen. You will go nowhere.

So I left South Africa for a long time. Because by 1994, vignerons in South Africa had stopped dreaming. They stopped being creative. They stopped having ambition because of the embargo. So they had no horizon. They were just here on the ground, looking at their own shoes. They were not looking out in the world. And I wanted to look like that.

So I left South Africa for some time to go work with the best guys in the world. I went to Germany first, and then Austria because of the language—it was easier to pick up. Then I went to Northern Italy and Alto Adige, also easy for the same reason. Then after that I went to France, then California, Oregon, and ended up in Spain.  

In France, I was first in the Côtes Catalanes, and then I went to stay for a harvest in Beaune with a friend of mine who was at a small domaine that doesn’t exist anymore. I’ve now been to Burgundy 30 times in my life, and have been drinking the wines of Burgundy since 1994. I spent a lot of time on Burgundy, all the little vineyards, all the little things, but also on Piedmont. It’s the other place I love.

Piedmont is Burgundy with more tannins and slightly more volatile acidity. I love Piedmont, but I also love all the wines of the world, the Mosel, the Pfalz, the Loire. But you have to learn to understand these wines.

I went also to Spain. I stayed almost 10 years in Spain.

And then I came back, and I worked for several years for two companies in South Africa. But I don’t work well in a commercial environment because every time I worked for someone, they said to me, “Eben, we want to make the best wine in the world. That’s what we’re going to do.”

And I’m like, “Okay, you want to make the best wine in the world? Let’s make the best wine in the world.”

But then they would start to cut corners. They want to make money. They’d look in the Excel spreadsheet, at the bottom right-hand corner. That’s where they are looking. They are not looking at the wine. They are looking at the numbers. You say to me, you want to make the best wine, but you’re looking at the numbers.

And if you’re looking at the numbers, then you’re not going to make the best wine. The best wine you make by looking at the vineyard, by looking at the wine, not looking at the numbers. The numbers come later, much later.

But first you must make the great wine. So I stopped working for other people in 2000, and I  founded this little domain.

For the first six years, I rented vineyards. And here on my property there was nothing but 10,000 eucalyptus trees. It was worth nothing.

But every year I started to pull out trees. Myself and two guys. Cut, burn, cut, burn, cut, burn. I was working in restaurants, I was working in wineries, I was doing consulting, I was even trading scrap metal just to get money. When I finally got some money, I got a machine to take out the tree stumps and burn them. Take out the roots and burn them. So this place burned for 10 years.

First you burn the top, then you burn the stumps, and then when all that is gone you have big rippers, and you rip out all the roots, which have the same quantity of material as the shoots and leaves and everything.

So this place burned three times as we took over.

I did that for 10 years, and then I started to plant different types of cereals and legumes to revitalize the soils. That, and a lot of compost, and a lot of work, and I only planted the first vineyards in 2015, after 10 years. 

In the meantime, I had other parcels that I worked that I didn’t own. I worked with other small monopoles everywhere at the same time I was developing this property, but my own vineyards only started in 2015.

With other people’s vineyards, I always did all the work. Because if I don’t grow the grapes, I don’t make the wine. For me, if you don’t work the soil, if you don’t work in the vineyard, then you don’t have the connectivity you need to make a better wine. I came out here because learning is my passion. I’m 53 this year. I’m still studying. I will never stop. It’s not passive studying, it’s active.

One of my passions is geology. On Monday last week, we just launched a map of the Swartland that I worked on for four years now. The first geological map of the appellation.

The reason the Swartland is so great is that it has the best geology in South Africa for wine. This mountain is all granite. It’s called the granite pluton, and granite is very good for red wine and white wine. You’ll find granite in the Roussillon and in the Dão in Portugal. You’ll find it in the Gredos mountains around Madrid, in Navarra. In Hermitage.  Many of the great wines in the world are made from granite. 

But all the sides, the hills around the sides, are all schist. Schist is very good for wine. You have it in the Douro, in Priorat, the Mosel, Ribeira Sacra, parts of the Wachau.

And then if you go over the mountain, you’ve got a big alluvial plain. Alluvial soils are not soils that were born there. They move with water. It’s a sedimentary soil. So we have a big alluvial plain going to Darling. We also have parts with deep clay, with iron and high in silica, similar to Bulgari in Tuscany, and then up north we have 100% limestone calcaire, like you find in Chablis and Burgundy and Jerez.

Then right in the middle of the Swartland we have the foot of a big mountain that is a big sandstone formation high in silica quartz.

So when you study geology globally, there is no appellation in the world that has all this in one appellation. Swartland is 990,000 hectares, and it’s got 15,400 hectares of vineyards, but the vineyards are all planted in these little microclimates that are perfect, and that’s why this place is so great, and it’s why I came here, because my study of geology helps me know exactly what soil can make what.

I work with a huge technical team – eight guys, the top eight guys in the world, and we fly satellites, and build three-dimensional solar radiation models, topography scales, GIS for airflow patterns, we scan the soil using electric resistivity tomography, and we map the soils and classify them.

So when we find a vineyard, we study it, and when we have a place where we want to plant, we also study it, and we plant it perfectly based on what we learn from the study. But sometimes there are already great things out there, and we find them too. 

That’s been my last 25 years. I spent a lot of energy to find the best vineyards in South Africa. Because with winemaking, you don’t make the best wine. You make the best wine with the best vineyard. And it’s been a huge process in the last 25 years to make sure we have the best vineyards. 

But then you need to know how to farm. Vititiculture is the biggest activity of our operation. We take 20% of our revenue every year and put it into research. 

Every year, 20%. It’s a big number. We run on about a 31% margin, so we keep about 11%, and we put 20% back into R&D. Now we have the vineyards, and we’re only starting to make really good wine with these vineyards. I can feel it coming—the energy is coming, it’s good now but in 20 years it will be unbelievable. I’m there in the stadium, putting on my shoes, getting on the blocks, not even running yet. Just getting the things ready so that we can go. 

I’ve been to most of the great and famous winegrowing regions in the world, and it’s never this diverse. If you cannot make a good wine in the Seartland, you must do something else. It’s finished for you. It’s such an amazing place.

I have friends in France making very good wine, but the places are difficult. To make good wine every year in Chinon or Vouvray, it’s difficult. The rain, the hail, the frost, the mildew. It’s tough in France. The French make the most perfect wines on the planet, and the Italians make the most emotional wines on the planet. And I hope one day we can make a wine that’s very emotional and really very well made. Perfect, I don’t know. I’m not so obsessed with perfection.

I’m more interested in making the wine of the place. But Alder, it comes back to this place, this space. Before we walk in the vineyards, I want to say, I studied biodynamics with Pierre Masson south of Burgundy, and I studied organics, and in 2001 I joined a big study group in America on Regenerative viticulture. We were already talking about it then. Now it is a fashionable word.

In that study group, I sat on the panel of climate change. It’s a big topic. Even in 2001, we were starting to realize how dramatic the change of climate will be globally. So we’ve been working with GIS—I have Jaco Engelbrecht, one of the best GIS specialists on viticulture, working here a day and a half every two weeks—and with the geologists to make a strategy for the future and for climate change. 

[Sadie gestures at the book Wine Grapes by José Vouillamoz, Jancis Robinson, and Julia Harding]

This has 1400 different grapes. But in the area between Crete and Lisbon we have 5000 grape varieties. Five thousand.  So when you think you have 5000 grapes in such a small geographical area (that part of Europe fits into Texas and Nevada), yet we planted New Zealand, Australia, South Africa, South America, North America, and China with basically seven grapes. 

Do you see the dilemma? The dilemma is that you cannot make the geometrics, the geophysics, the geology, the topography, and the climatology of six continents work with just seven grapes. It’s impossible. 

You cannot argue against data. It doesn’t matter how clever you are. You cannot argue against data and statistics. You are out.

So I started in 2002 to import the best plants I could find for this place. And what is the best plant?

In the vine kingdom, you have two types of plants: isohydric and anisohydric. With an anisohydric vine, when it’s getting very warm and dry, the plants start to evaporate a lot of water. And the roots cannot take up water at the same rate as the evaporation. So the plant goes into negative hydric pressure.

The isohydric vine [in the same situation] shuts down the stomata on the bottom of the leaf. The stomata are the respiratory organs of the vines. The vine shuts down the process of evapotranspiration, and it puts on standby photosynthesis and energy accumulation between, say 11:00 AM and 2:30 PM in the day. Three and a half hours on standby. 

Anisohydric is the exact opposite. They evapotranspire too much; the roots cannot take up the same amount of water, and they dehydrate.

So our focus is on isohydric plants, and the selection of isohydric plants in the Old World, which is what we started to do in 2002. To figure out whether a vine is isohydric, you have to test it with a leaf [pressure] bomb test. We have an apparatus for this. And you must test it over the whole season.

So we went to get the best isohydric grapes in the world. Assyrtiko, Agiorgitiko, Grillo, Catarratto, Fiano, Clairette Blanche, Grenache Blanc, Cinsault Blanc, Picpoul de Pinet, Grenache, Carignan, Cinsault Noir, Cunoise, Terret Noire, Vermentino. These are all very good isohydrics. And we planted a lot of them, at first in experimental patches, and it took us from 2002 to 2019, seventeen years, to do the research.

And then in 2018 we planted the first commercial vineyards with these varieties.

The other aspect we have in vines is epigenetics. The grapevine is one of the plants in the world that can mutate the fastest. It can make mutations for itself without altering the DNA of the plant, and the word for this is epigenetics. 

You probably know that Chenin Blanc has been in South Africa for 300 years. Did you know that in the Loire Valley, Chenin Blanc is an anisohydric vine. But here in South Africa, Chenin Blanc is isohydric. 

Here’s another example. Trousseau in the Jura in France is anisohydric. But it made its way to Portugal, where it is called Bastardo, and in Portugal, it is isohydric. It’s adapted to the drought.  The Trousseau in California is also isohydric, because it came from Portugal about a hundred years ago. 

Isohydric plants help us keep the alcohol levels down. We stay under 14%. We have good pH. We have good acidity. We have freshness, linearity, transparency.  We have precision in our wines. Because if you pick grapes at 15% alcohol. you lose the definition.

I have a friend who works in Dijon, in a lab where a lot of the wines go to be analyzed. She cannot tell me many things because it’s private, but she can share the broad statistics, and alcohol levels are 2% higher than they were 15 years ago. I don’t mind paying 500 Euros for a great bottle of Burgundy, but I’m not going to pay that for a wine at 15% alcohol. I’m not going to pay for a 16% alcohol Barolo either.

Needless to say, we’ve been doing a lot of massale selection on grape varieties that have been in areas for a long time with the right characteristics, because of this aspect of adaptation to a place. 

And after you make a massale selection, what is the most important thing? To make sure that the material is virus-free. So we have a laboratory (it’s not our laboratory; we contract with them) to do tissue culture. We do in vitro tissue culture. When a plant grows, the tip of the plant, the upper epidermis, is new, and it takes 24 hours for any virus in the plant to infect new cells.

So we cut microscopically there, cut out the cells, and put them in an agar medium and let them grow, and then you cut again, and reculture, and that way you can eventually get rid of the virus. It takes a long time, and it’s expensive, but when we do a good massale selection, we want to make sure the material is clean.

America, where you live, Alder, is frankly a shit show. You Americans all go from California to Burgundy, and you brag that you cut your Pinot Noir from Romanée-Conti or Rousseau or whatever. You go and cut it and put it in the bag and take it back, but what do you take back? Virus. You people don’t know what you’re doing. You’re fucked.

That’s why you have red blotch, Flavescence dorée, Pierce’s Disease, esca. You have everything. its just bullshit. That’s not how you make a great vineyard.

We spent a lot of energy in research to make the foundation of this domain. I’m only interested in foundation. We took every Euro we had for 25 years and put it in the vineyards.

We’ve only had this new winery for 2 years. Before then, we were making wine in a shed.

This cellar was a big project three years ago, but this doesn’t change the wine. Zero. It’s a nice place to come and sit and have tea or whatever, but the cellar doesn’t change the wine. 

Today we have on the domain 22 hectares of vineyards, and we have another 29 hectares that we lease. So, in total, around 51 hectares. But we don’t use all the fruit. We also sell some fruit to leading producers. We only use about 80%.

We are still working everything on gobelet. The big reason is, you know, they say the modern era of wine is the last 8000 years. It started in Georgia, Armenia, and Iran, right? And the vines came from there to Europe. So there’s been a lot of movement in 8000 years, and for the last 8000 years, this [head-trained or bush vine pruning] is how all vines were grown before.

The wires on the poles? Those are new. Only for about 120 years have we had wires on the pole—this vertical shoot positioning.

So why don’t we do it? Vertical shoot positioning was designed to mechanize vineyards, to improve the ease of working, manage yield control, all aimed at uniformity and efficiency of work, and to improve ripening. 

The problem with VSP is that the canopy is very narrow, and you have a lot more evapotranspiration because you have a lot more leaves. You increase your leaf surface area, and you increase your water loss. So what happens when you put vines on VSP? You’ve created this artificial system that now has increased evapotranspiration, and so what do you have to do? You have to irrigate. You have to put in another artificial intervention. And irrigation requires energy to pump water, energy we don’t have here in South Africa.

So from a sustainability perspective, irrigation in agriculture in the long term, excessive irrigation, is not a sustainable answer. And with wine, the idea is to bottle a particular milesime, but when you irrigate, you start to lose [the characteristics of] the milesime. Your wines become monolithic.

Also, when you irrigate, you bring all the roots to the surface. The roots don’t go deep; they stay here where the water is. It’s like trust funds for kids. They usually don’t work out. Because life is too easy. Where is the character going to come from?

For us, irrigation is a no-go.

Also, we plant our vineyards square [equidistant between all plants]. With a trellis, you have high density here [in the row itself] and low density in between [in the gaps between the rows]. And you get what we call partial root zone development. 

The roots are always where all your compaction is. So we have a system instead where we plant our vineyard square, where you have a 360-degree dynamic of root zone development. And then with gobelet, you have a 360-degree canopy too. 

It’s like trees in nature. They are always like the number eight. What you have on the bottom, you have on the top [the same amount of plant mass above and below the ground]. When you plant VSP, you have something more like a 9. With a big canopy and vines that send their roots all into the space between the rows. Vines will never grow towards each other; they are too competitive.

So we have 360 degrees of growth, where the vines are each in their own circle. And then you can run a tractor in any direction, so you can change where it goes and you don’t get the same compaction year after year.

We use a lot of mulching for the climate [to retain moisture]. We plant a lot of cover crops. This year was fava beans to help with nitrogen and phosphates, and when it grows up, we roll it flat.

When you have a lot of grass on the ground, you keep the solar radiation off the ground, and you limit the evapotranspiration. You keep your moisture. Also your temperature is more homogenous. The third thing is weed control. You create shade and the weeds can’t grow in the shade. You do your weed control with shade. And lastly, the cover crop is all carbon that will go back into the soil to build better soil for next year. Because if you can increase your carbon percentage in your soil, you increase your water holding capacity, your mineral capacity. 

We plant blends. We don’t make blends in the cellar or on the table, we make them in the vineyard. If you blend in the cellar on the table, you are starting to work with your brain. You’re starting to think about the Wine Advocate, or what Alder is going to write in his report. About consumer expectation, about ego.

No, I’m here growing wine. We are wine growers, not wine makers. 

When we have 20 years of wines to taste through, a vertical, I don’t want 300 different notes saying, “This year I did this to the wine, this year I did that.”

I want to simply say, “This vineyard, what did this vineyard do for each of these 20 years?”  This vineyard, not me, not my technicians—this vineyard.

We farm organically, but I will never put it anywhere on the bottle. As for biodynamics, I like biodynamie, I just don’t like biodynamists. They are so fucking dogmatic. Dogma kills the brain. Rudolph Steiner was not the last clever guy on the planet. I work with a guy here, Dr. Strauss, he’s fucking 20 times more clever than Steiner. We cannot stop our thinking as of 1924.

If I put 500 and 501 on the vineyard, then I’m a cool kid. I can get 20 extra Euros a bottle. Fuck that. It’s like silver bullets and recipes. No, you have to use your brain. You must keep developing your viticulture. You must keep developing your plant material. You must keep developing your team, the team that does the work. That’s the business. Not the business of doing paperwork, of having all the consultants come in and file their forms. Fuck that. It will never work for me. I’m not making wine for them. I make wine to make the best wine I can, and I will use whatever resource I can get my hands on.

It would be good for the organic movement for me to be certified. But the organic movement is not my movement. My movement is wine. 

For winemaking, the white grapes come in, and they get chilled for the night to six degrees [Celsius]. The red grapes come in and go into the destemmer.

We make every white wine the same, and every red wine the same. Always, because when we taste the wines, we don’t want to taste the winemaking, we want to see the vineyards. When you do research, or any clinical trial, the most important thing is your control from which you will make every measurement. And if you have too much variability, you will never know what you do.

So winemaking here is very easy. The whites are pressed with whole clusters in the pneumatic press, and everything [including all the lees] goes into the tank. The reds always have 30% whole cluster no matter what. Never higher, never lower, and they are all basket-pressed, and we use all of the press juice, no fractions, no press cuts.

The whites and reds ferment in concrete. Each individual vineyard gets its own permanent tank where it ferments each year. Each tank has its own microflora, but just as importantly, once we’ve figured out a system, we don’t have to figure it out again. The wines are aged in a combination of amphorae, concrete and large oak foudres, or occasionally, only in foudre.

The winery is designed with energy efficiency and water efficiency. We use all the water that falls on the roofs. And then the water we use in the cellar we put back into our gardens, and into our water purification plant, which makes water perfect for the house, the cellar, the people.

Up top we have a huge solar plant with 2 megawatts generation. We use one of those megawatts, and the other goes into a battery bank for storage. Since 2022, we are completely off the grid.

And with that, it was time to taste.

Tasting Notes

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “Skerpioen” White Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of freshly shucked oysters, lemon zest, and lime blossom. In the mouth, saline lime blossom, citrus pith, oyster shell, and pulverized stone flavors have incredible crystalline acidity, lift, and dynamism. Utterly delicious and nearly impossible not to swallow. A 50-50 blend of Chenin Blanc and Palomino grown on calcareous soils. 13.5% alcohol. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $87. click to buy.

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “Kokerboom” Semillon, Citrusdal Mountain, Olifants River, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon oil, lemon peel, and wet chalkboard. In the mouth, pure crystalline flavors of lemon peel, lemon oil, crushed stones, and sunlight have a gorgeous stony grip and chalky texture in the mouth, along with outstanding acidity. Very faintly saline with hints of bee pollen and acacia blossom lingering in the finish. Stunning. There are 5 ancient Semillon vineyards in the country, and this is one of them, with vines around 100 years old. 14% alcohol. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $86. click to buy.

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “Skurfburg” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear and pear skin, white flowers, and wet chalkboard. In the mouth, salty flavors of pear and crushed stones mix with grapefruit pith, a touch of nougat, flower pollen, and chamomile. The wine has fantastic acidity, an amazing crushed stone grip on the palate, and incredible length. Phenomenal. Grown in very dry sandstone soils at high elevation. 13.5% alcohol. 4000 bottles made. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $79. click to buy.

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “Twiswind” White Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of citrus pith, lemon peel, yellow flowers, and a hint of dried herbs. In the mouth, faintly saline flavors of citrus peel, citrus pith, crushed stone, and herbs have a lightly grippy, chalky texture and excellent acidity. There’s also a hint of green herbs in the finish. A field blend of Vermentino, Picpoul, Marsanne, Grenache Blanc, Cinsaut Blanc, Palomino, Chenin Blanc, Grillo, Assyrtiko, Verdelho, Clairette Blanche, and Semillon from one of Sadie’s new estate vineyards, his most wind-affected site. Twiswind means “to argue with the wind.” This is the first commercial bottling of this estate vineyard. 13.5% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $93. click to buy.

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “T’Voetpad” White Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon-scented quartz crystals, wet chalkboard, and oyster shell. In the mouth, salty flavors of lemon oil, wet pavement, pulverized stones, and white flowers have a lovely stony grip and gorgeous, crackling acidity. Flavors seem to linger and shimmer for a long time on the palate. A frankly jaw-dropping wine of unbelievable deliciousness. A blend of Semillon Blanc, Semillon Gris, Muscat, and Chenin Blanc grown on alluvial sandstone. This is the oldest coplantation of white grapes in South Africa, planted in 1878. 14% alcohol. 2200 bottles made each year. Score: around 10. Cost: $118. click to buy.

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “Mev. Kirsten” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in color, this wine smells of pear, lemon oil, pear skin, and white flowers. In the mouth, pear and white flowers, pear skin, and crushed stones are salty, stony, crystalline, and gorgeous. There’s a hint of green herbs and white flowers in the finish, but overall this wine conveys an impression of drinking liquid, scented stone, which tinkles like icicles thawing on a sunny winter’s day. Positively thrilling with incredible acidity. This is the oldest Chenin Blanc vineyard in South Africa, planted in 1905. 14% alcohol. Score: around 10. Cost: $175. click to buy.

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “Rotsbank” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of salty wet chalkboard and pear skin with just a hint of struck match. In the mouth, stony and salty citrus pith and unripe pear flavors mix with pear skin and crushed quartz crystals. Stunningly lean and crystalline with amazing acidity. Grown in blue granite on the Paardeberg, a very unusual site. Rotsbank means “rock shelf.” 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $90. click to buy.

2023 The Sadie Family Wines “Palladius” White Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon peel, pear skin, nectarine, fynbos, and wet chalkboard. In the mouth, salty flavors of fynbos, lemon peel, grapefruit, dried herbs, nectarine, and a hint of white flowers have a weightlessness to them. This wine is deeply stony and wonderfully salty with a faint waxy character that lingers in the finish. Shimmering, crystalline, ethereal, and gobsmackingly tasty, with phenomenal acidity. Made from 16 different vineyards, all dedicated solely to this Palladius wine. A blend of Chenin Blanc, Grenache Blanc, Clairette Blanche, Viognier, Verdelho, Roussanne, Marsanne, Semillon Gris, Semillon Blanc, Palomino, Colombard, Grillo and Assyrtiko. For the first time in this wine, a small vineyard planted next to Skerpioen is being used for 20% of the blend, which is planted to Assyrtiko, Verdelho, Vermentino, Grenache Blanc, and Chenin Blanc, all grown in pure limestone. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 10. Cost: $139. click to buy.

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “Soldaat” Grenache, Citrusdal Mountain, Olifants River, South Africa
Light ruby in the glass, this wine smells of wildflowers, sour cherries, fynbos, and strawberries. In the mouth, strawberry and herb flavors mix electrically with sour cherries, chopped green herbs, citrus peel, and wet stones. Saline and delicious. Fine-grained tannins hang gauzily in the background as incredible acidity makes for a seemingly endless finish. Gorgeous and mouthwatering. Grown in sandstone soils. 13.3% alcohol. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $74. click to buy.

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “Sonvang” Red Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Medium garnet in the glass with ruby highlights, this wine smells of black tea, wildflowers, sour cherries, and raspberries. In the mouth, sour cherries, raspberries, dried herbs, fynbos, and black tea flavors are wrapped in a fleecy sheet of tannins that coat the mouth. Notes of fynbos herbs linger in the finish. Amazing acidity. A field blend of Alicante Bouschet, Agiorgitiko, Pontac, Bastardo do Castillo, Trincadera, Tinta Barocca, Lledoner Pelut, Grenache Noir, Pinotage, Cinsaut, Counoise, and Carignan. Sonvang means “sun catcher.” This is the first commercial bottling of this estate vineyard. 14% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $86. click to buy.

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “Pofadder” Cinsault, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Medium garnet with a hint of haze to it, this wine smells of sour cherry, dried herbs, and citrus peel. In the mouth, sour cherry and redcurrant flavors mix with citrus peel, lemon juice, and dried herbs. Gorgeous, bright, saline, and textured with gauzy tannins and fantastic acidity. Notes of fynbos linger in the finish. Wonderfully stony, aromatic and bright. 41-year-old vines planted on slate. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $83. click to buy.

2024 The Sadie Family Wines “Treinspoor” Tinta Barrocca, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherry, sour cherry, licorice, and chopped green herbs. In the mouth, fleecy tannins coat the mouth, while black cherry, plum, citrus peel, dried herbs, and pulverized stones vibrate with excellent acidity. Minty in quality, with chopped green herbs lingering in the finish. Mysterious and compelling. Planted in 1974 in alluvial soils. 13.1% alcohol. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $85. click to buy.

2023 The Sadie Family Wines “Columella” Red Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of violets, black cherries, blackberries, licorice, and blueberries. In the mouth, gorgeous, mouthwatering flavors of fynbos, wildflowers, mulberries, citrus peel, and licorice root are swirling and dynamic on the palate. Fresh, delicious, and saline, with just the barest hint of dashi-like umami and fantastic acidity. A blend of Syrah, Mourvèdre, Grenache, Carignan, Cinsaut, Tinta Barocca, and Pinotage. From 12 vineyards, 11 of which are solely dedicated to Columella. 13.5% alcohol. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $146. click to buy.

2004 The Sadie Family Wines “Columella” Red Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Dark ruby in the glass, this wine smells of dates, raisins, chocolate, and licorice mixed with cherries and a hint of acetone that eventually morphs into wild floral and aromatic herb aromas. In the mouth, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of salty licorice and dried black cherries. Dried herbs and dried flowers linger in the finish. The wine is long and supple in the mouth, with excellent acidity remaining after 21 years. 14.5% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $n/a

title: Is That the Death Rattle of Wine Writing I Hear?
summary:
The purpose of any honest writing competition can only be to support and encourage the craft and industry of writing.

The post Is That the Death Rattle of Wine Writing I Hear? appeared first on Vinography.
content:
The purpose of any honest writing competition can only be to support and encourage the craft and industry of writing. Unfortunately, the times we live in now require three crucial words to be added to that statement. The purpose of any honest writing competition can only be to support and encourage the craft and industry of writing by human beings.

On September 11th, the most prestigious wine communication competition, the 67 Pall Mall Global Wine Communicator Awards, awarded one of its writing prizes to a piece of work that seems to have been written entirely by AI. Understandably, the wine writing “industry,” such as it is, has responded vociferously with a measure of both outrage and disbelief. I recommend reading the pieces by Henry Jeffrys, Felicity Carter, Joe Roberts, Alice Feiring, and Peter Pharos to get a sense of the response to date.

I’ve personally been waiting to see how the organizers of the competition would handle the situation. The totality of their response, provided not in any official statement but merely in quotes to some of the inquiring journalists listed above, appears to consist of the following:

  • A defense of the judges and judging process while clearly pointing out that the contest rules did not explicitly forbid AI (which is true)
  • A defense of the piece’s contributor, who, they imply, has maintained it was not written entirely by AI
  • A professed lack of confidence in AI-detection software and a suggestion that the author’s personal style is naturally similar to the supposed telltale signs of AI writing
  • A suggestion that many people criticising the award decision simply do not like the piece of writing, and that perhaps “they are not the intended audience” for the work

When approached by some of the journalists above, the contributor of the piece in question has declined to comment and referred inquiries back to the contest organizers.

Let’s return to the (hopefully uncontroversial) premise that any writing awards program in existence would aim to support, encourage, develop, promote, and celebrate quality writing by human beings. After all, the name of the specific award program in question includes the word “communicator,” suggesting some entity doing the communication that we shouldn’t be too hard-pressed to assume is a human individual.

All that being the case, it seems to me that the only policy when it comes to the use of AI in a contest such as this would be one of ZERO TOLERANCE.

You simply cannot be in the business of recognizing the efforts and craft of writers and simultaneously be willing to accept and evaluate work that was substantially, let alone entirely, created by artificial intelligence.

This is not to say that writers should not be able to utilize AI as a tool in their process.

You want AI to check your grammar? Fine. You want it to give you suggestions on how to better structure your argument to be persuasive? Great. Need an idea for a metaphor that might achieve your goals? Go ahead and get some advice from your favorite chatbot. But when it comes to the words that end up on the page in consideration for awards, prize money, and accolades, those need to be produced by a human being. Period.

The fact that an explicit AI policy was not in place, therefore, does not seem to be a reasonable excuse for tolerance of AI-generated work as a contender for the awards. That seems tantamount to accepting that Rosie Ruiz was well within her rights to hop into a taxi for the last six miles of the 1980 Boston Marathon. The race rules definitely didn’t say she couldn’t do that.

It seems to me that when faced with allegations (substantiated by multiple results from AI detection software) that a piece selected by the judges was mostly or entirely written by AI, the folks at the 67 Pall Mall Awards had only two plausible courses of action to maintain the credibility of their awards program.

Option one was to publicly and officially acknowledge the controversy; offer a mea culpa for not having had a policy forbidding AI work in place; and then proceed to run every finalist piece of work through an AI detector and revise their awards decisions based on the outcome of those tests. Of course, if those tests were inconclusive or ambiguous, no revision need be made.

Option two was to publicly and officially acknowledge the controversy; offer a mea culpa for not having had a policy forbidding AI work in place; and then state clearly that while they are declining to revise their award decisions already communicated this year, they will have a zero-tolerance policy for AI-created work moving forward.

I would certainly have advocated for the first option.

Unfortunately, the organizers have chosen to do neither of those two things, and have made it clear in response to my inquiries that they will not even be issuing an official statement on the situation to everyone who submitted work to the contest, let alone to the public at large.

This is disappointing and, in my opinion, not the way to handle what has clearly become a public relations crisis that threatens the integrity of the awards program itself and undermines the very craft the organizers purport to celebrate.

In the face of this seeming inaction, I’ve gone ahead and run the text of all six finalists for this award through GPTZero, which I believe to be the best AI-detection software in the business. The results, which you can see below (click to enlarge), are stark.

Five of the pieces come back rated as being 100% human-written. One, the chosen winner of this award, comes back as 100% AI-written. This is a detector that measures the presence and influence of AI in single-percentage increments.

The definitiveness of this result cannot be minimized or brushed away by conversations about software quality and on-trend writing styles.

Let me offer some additional, more detailed perspective. I spent my entire professional career in the technology and design world, running a full-service digital marketing agency for two decades. I have been an early adopter and student of AI. I use it daily, and in so doing, save myself tens of hours of work per week, including getting feedback and advice on my own writing from time to time. And while I use it to generate art for my site, such as the image at top, I do not use it to generate content published under my byline here or anywhere else. But I use it. A lot.

More specifically, I used AI-writing detectors extensively for more than 2 years to evaluate the personal statements submitted along with scholarship applications to the Glancy Wine Education Foundation, which has a zero-tolerance AI policy for these statements. That work has involved evaluating hundreds of pieces of writing in that time period with many different tools, eventually leading me to my chosen piece of software and a serious degree of confidence in its capabilities.

I can tell you definitively that the best of these tools are really, really good. Are they infallible? Of course not, but they have gotten very sophisticated and nuanced in their evaluation capabilities, which, as I mentioned, can be expressed at incremental percentage points of confidence. They are absolutely and readily able to distinguish between text that has been modified by AI, text that contains only some AI content, and text that was produced wholesale by AI. These tools are not thrown off by short sentences, word cadence, em-dashes, or overly snappy writing. By way of example, one of the other finalists I evaluated above was an honest-to-goodness poem, and it was scored as being 100% human-written.

In my judgment, the 67 Pall Mall Awards have a serious problem that they have chosen not to fully resolve. They have been quoted in at least one of the pieces above as saying that they are formulating an AI policy for next year, but hearing in 8 months that next year’s awards won’t allow AI (let’s pray, shall we?) will be cold consolation to the people who lost to a chatbot this year. I seriously hope none of them paid their own hard-earned money for a plane ticket to attend the awards ceremony in London as a finalist.

What’s more, I can’t shake the feeling that this isn’t just a story about a wine-writing contest fallen victim to the pitfalls of an AI-enabled world. It’s a symptom of a profession slowly being strangled.

I have not been one of those people crying that AI is coming for all our jobs. I’m very optimistic by nature, and that optimism extends to the possibilities that AI, properly utilized and controlled, offers for humanity.

But let’s face it, wine writing as a profession has been dying a long, drawn-out death. This situation, in which the arguably most prominent arbiter of quality in the craft of wine writing is awarding £3000 in cash to a piece of writing clearly written by AI, feels like yet one more nail in the coffin of a profession not long for this world.

It has always been extremely difficult to make a living as a wine writer. That was true when I started writing about wine 22 years ago. It has only gotten worse. Much worse.

In the span of time I’ve been writing about wine, the world of print journalism has been decimated. According to a report commissioned by the Library of Congress, newspaper ad revenue dropped roughly 80% from a peak of $73.2 billion in 2000 to just $6 billion in 2023. In roughly the same period, 3,500 newspapers ceased publication. Print magazine advertising spend dropped roughly 70% in the same period, according to Statista.com.

Thank you, Google Ads.

I can still remember a time when the newspapers in most major metropolitan areas had wine columns. No longer.

Salaried wine writers represent a nearly extinct species. Even at the most storied publications, including my employer Jancisrobinson.com and Decanter, most content is generated by freelancers who get piece rates and receive zero benefits.

When 60 to 80 hours of work driving around wine country to taste and conduct interviews nets a freelance wine writer $300 for 1300 words, and no expense reimbursement (real rates, real facts, people), is it any wonder that fewer and fewer educated, knowledgeable people can even contemplate doing that kind of work?

Congratulations on spending the time and money for a four-year college degree in journalism. Now go get a job waiting tables. Here’s what one of our greatest living wine writers makes per year.

No, these days, wine writing is increasingly left to dilettantes with other income sources, many of whom have different standards for quality and no allegiance to (or sometimes even knowledge of) journalistic ethics. They’re content to get a press trip here and there, and to make a couple of hundred dollars per month from their Substack subscriptions (by the way, Substack sucks).

Is it any wonder, then, that we’ve seen the sharp rise of the influencer set, who, provided they amass enough followers, can get paid $3000 for a “collab” with a brand that involves visiting a winery and popping a cork on camera while extolling the virtues of that particular slice of wine country? It’s a great gig if you can get it, but that’s advocacy-based marketing, not journalism.

Wine criticism, too, seems to be fading from relevance. Who really wants to read hundreds of tasting notes anymore? Not the young, up-and-coming wine lovers of tomorrow. They’re getting recommendations from their friends, from TikTok, and of course, from AI, which is helpfully trained on the work of all those underpaid wine writers. I don’t have any data about the subscriber bases of the specialty wine publications that trade in ratings and reviews, but I’d put some serious money on them being flat or declining, even as more and more outlets spring up to slowly fracture the audience for scores into more and more selective niches. We’ve come a long way from the days of the ParkTator.

The production side of the wine industry, which so desperately depends on wine writing and criticism, isn’t helping a bit. The roughly 11,000 wineries in the US (and countless more abroad) all want their wines scored by various publications, but most of those wineries don’t even bother to subscribe to the very publications from which they are hoping to receive coverage.

Every month, without fail, wineries whose wines I have reviewed for Jancis Robinson shamelessly ask me if I can give them a PDF of the paywalled article and wine scores, which they presumably plan on republishing with glee on their own websites and social media accounts. The degree to which the wine industry wants its cake without being willing to pay for the plate on which it is served demonstrates a staggering level of blindness and entitlement.

There is almost no one left to pay anything resembling a living wage for those who want to write about wine professionally. Fewer and fewer people therefore will write about wine, and the quality of the writing that does get done will necessarily suffer.

We are on this very downhill slide without a doubt. Where we are on the slope, and its precise angle of incline, remain fodder for much debate.

Can the problem be fixed? Sure. Just like the declining quality of our education system in the US can be fixed as soon as we start funding it well enough so that teachers can afford to live in the communities where they teach, and they don’t have to ask parents to donate pencils to their classrooms so kids can have something to write with.

Unfortunately, in neither case am I holding my breath. But the 67 Pall Mall Awards needn’t wait for the wine industry to wake up and smell the coffee. They could start by declaring that the next £3000 they hand out will, guaranteed, be celebrating real human creativity. That much, at least, is entirely within their control.

By way of disclosure, I was a finalist for one of the 67 Pall Mall awards this year (Long-form Writing) and was also short-listed, but not a finalist, in the Short-Form category, which is the subject of this article. I have also been shortlisted for these awards in previous years.

title: Hip-Hop Doesn’t Need Wine, But Wine Just Might Need Hip-Hop
summary:
Despite the fading evening light on Lankershim Boulevard, I had to squint a bit in the dim light of the

The post Hip-Hop Doesn’t Need Wine, But Wine Just Might Need Hip-Hop appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Despite the fading evening light on Lankershim Boulevard, I had to squint a bit in the dim light of the club. The wide-open floor was already beginning to fill up with fashionably dressed people as the sounds of hip-hop coursed through the club’s speakers at a relatively subdued volume.

A glance around the room suggested the action was on the periphery, where several individuals stood behind small tables each holding a couple of wine bottles. I grabbed a proffered wine glass from a side table (noting with a somewhat delayed shock that it was a Zalto Universal) and headed for my first taste, walking up to a table staffed by a young woman wearing a hoodie. With a pleasant hello and a smile, Saskia de Rothschild poured me a taste of 1985 Lafite, and that is when I knew I was in for a wine event unlike anything else I had ever experienced.

This was Vin et Hip-Hop Los Angeles, the first US version of a wine event originally held in 2022 at the venerable Château du Clos de Vougeot in Burgundy. The event sprang from a collaboration between vintner Jeremy Seysses of Domaine Dujac, podcaster and educator Jermaine “Wolf of Wine” Stone, and Milena Berman and Loïc Lamy, the duo behind the experiential marketing agency Hautes Côtes. In its first incarnations, it brought hip-hop performers to the heart of Burgundy for a music-festival-meets-wine-tasting event celebrating two expressions of craft that have historically had only the most tenuous of relationships.

The Birth of Vin et Hip-Hop

As a recent Art History graduate working in Los Angeles art galleries, the young California-born Milena Berman jumped at the chance when she received an offer to join an art tourism company based in Burgundy.

“Three weeks later, sight unseen, I moved to Beaune,” she said when I interviewed her in March. It was something of a dream job, creating bespoke tours to art fairs and museums all over Europe for high-level donors to top museums around the world. But like so many things during the Pandemic, it all came crashing to a halt. Berman looked around at her options and decided she might be able to work in wine.

“I reached out to Domaine Dujac, and I said, I’m not sure what I can do at a winery, maybe marketing and sales,” she recalled. “And they were like, ‘Yeah, we don’t do marketing and sales.'”

But the family clearly saw something in the young woman and found her a position on the administrative side of the business, working closely with winemaker Jeremy Seysses, particularly on activities supporting The Roots Fund, something meaningful to her as an American in the midst of the #BlackLivesMatter movement and moment.

As the world opened back up, Berman decided to leave Dujac and launch her own agency, Hautes Côtes, with partner Loïc Lamy, but just before she did, she ended up helping Dujac put on an event that featured podcaster Jermaine Stone. Berman and Stone hit it off and began discussing other potential events they could collaborate on, and they settled on the idea of a post-harvest party.

“I said to Jermaine that I’d make grilled cheese sandwiches and we could find a DJ, and he could do the playlist for the event, and I could ask Jeremy [Seysses] and a few other winemakers to pour a white wine, and so we made a terrible little logo, and made an announcement, and it sold out in minutes,” said Berman. “We were like, ‘Who’s coming to this?'”

Young interns from all over the world staying in Burgundy for their harvest jobs snapped up many of the inexpensive tickets, but some were locals, like Dominique Lafon.

“Dominique said, ‘This is amazing, next year you have to do it at Clos de Vougeot,’ and we were like, ‘Yeah, right,’ and he said, ‘No, I’m serious, I will go with you and tell them they should do this,'” recalls Berman.

Come as You Are

With Lafon’s urging, the Château du Clos de Vougeot agreed, and Vin et Hip Hop was born. When word came through the grapevine that Mike D was coming to Burgundy to be inducted into the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin, the opportunity proved too good to pass up. Introductions were made, and the Beastie Boys founder agreed to DJ the inaugural event following his induction.

From the outset, the organizers envisioned an experience with far more accessibility than the black-tie affairs that have made the Château du Clos de Vougeot legendary among wine lovers.

“We were like, ‘Come in your jeans, come as you are,'” said Berman, “and we wanted the tickets to be less than 100 bucks with dinner included.” The organizers set aside a portion of the proceeds to benefit The Roots Fund.

The resulting event was certainly unlike anything that the Château had ever hosted: 700 young people (and a few older folks, too) partying to the sounds of hip-hop while tasting Burgundies from top producers. In a model that has continued through all subsequent events, producers made bottles available for sale to attendees, who, in the fashion of La Paulée, could open them and share with friends, acquaintances, and strangers throughout the night.

“We talk about how wine can reach different audiences, but sometimes wine needs help,” said Icy Liu, of Becky Wasserman & Co., one of the event’s sponsors. “Wine has had a very different way of relating and representing itself and being engaged with culture in a certain way for a long time, but it’s maybe a bit out of touch with the mainstream of the culture. Hip-hop is cool. The artists are always driving the dialogue with what we’re wearing, where we’re eating, and what we’re doing. Hip-hop is shaping cultural identity.”

That sense of connection with mainstream culture, as well as the passionate communities that have arisen around hip-hop, became a core tenet of the event, which now describes one of its primary goals as “bridging worlds through cultural exchange.”

In addition to the several editions of the event held at Clos de Vougeot, the organizers have also put on Pop et Hip-Hop in the Champagne region. After several years of European events, American wine and hip-hop lovers clamored for a domestic version, and in a lobbying campaign that I imagine was something like the competition for Olympic host cities, Los Angeles won the right to host the first event on American soil.

A Los Angeles Exclusive

The 2026 event in Los Angeles at Verse was unlike any wine event I’ve attended across a number of dimensions. The wines being poured for attendees were spectacular: Vintage Krug Champagne, Billecart-Salmon Elisabeth Salmon Rosé, Domaine de Montille 1er Cru Les Sizies, Dalla Valle Maya, Harlan Estate, Colgin IX Estate, Jaboulet Hermitage La Chapelle, Château Lafleur, Comtes Lafon 1er Cru Meursault-Charmes, Domaine Dujac 1er Cru Aux Combottes, Michel Lafarge Volnay, Domaine Fourrier 1er Cru Combe aux Moines Gevrey-Chambertin, and yes, 1985 Château Lafite Rothschild, among many others.

The crowd was impressively diverse, in both age and race, and the vibe was electric even before the performers took the stage. Common, Keyon Harrold, Dominique Sanders, Jason L. Martin, Dilated Peoples, and a guest appearance from Wiz Khalifa kept the room thumping until late, while the parking lot was filled with food trucks dishing up everything from smash burgers to caviar bumps.

A team of sommeliers behind the bar handled an enthusiastic crowd of spendy wine lovers who were more than happy to deplete the stocks of wines from Burgundy, Champagne, Napa, Bordeaux, Abruzzo, and the Rhône being sold at eye-poppingly excellent prices. Not to unnecessarily tantalize you, but a 2021 Arnoux-Lachaux Vosne-Romanée was on offer that night for $250. Try to find that bottle at retail today, and you’ll pay somewhere north of $600.

The catch to all this was the price of entry. This party and concert (which Hautes Côtes flew me down to LA to attend) had no tickets. Attendance was by invitation only. And to secure an invitation, you had to purchase a seat at one of the many winemaker dinners that preceded the event, with price tags starting at $850 and going up to more than $2,500. I believe the capacity of the club topped out at around 200 people.

Standing there with a $78 hand-blown wine glass filled with $500-per-bottle Burgundy, watching Common freestyle his way through a verse about drinking wine, I didn’t exactly feel part of anything close to “the mainstream.” I was lucky enough to attend an event the likes of which few people have ever had the opportunity to experience. Rarified doesn’t begin to describe it, and that struck me as quite the opposite of what Vin et Hip Hop was trying to achieve, significant donations to The Roots Fund notwithstanding.

When I put this to winemaker Jeremy Seysses and to Berman, they both agreed that the level of exclusivity featured in this event was not in alignment with the mission and vision for Vin et Hip-Hop long term, and reflected more of the specific opportunity they had to partner with the Verse supper club, owned by Grammy-award-winning sound engineer Manny Marroquin.

“I want to see something much bigger in the US,” said Seysses, “closer to or even bigger than what we do at Clos de Vougeot, with similar ticket prices.”

I’d love to see that, too.

A Deserving Synergy

At a time when wine seems to be struggling for relevance with younger generations of drinkers, and demand is shrinking, the appeal of Vin et Hip-Hop becomes obvious. Making inroads with hip-hop’s own diverse audience, and more specifically Black wine drinkers, seems not just smart but imperative. Taking wine off its pedestal and putting it in contexts where it connects with other dimensions of culture offers an opportunity to have different conversations or even just experience wine in different moods. A festival called Blood of Gods, named after a ‘zine of the same name, is doing something similar with heavy metal music in Washington State.

Can events such as these truly change the world of wine, a few hundred people at a time? That remains to be seen. At the very least, they represent something novel and exciting in an industry that seems convinced we’ll all be enthused by a press release touting the latest 90-point scores or the achievement of a new sustainability certification.

Wine needs to be more fun. And it needs to be more fun to a lot more people than it has in the past if the industry is going to survive and thrive. It also needs to connect with communities of passion, and especially those that have at their center things other than wine itself.

Wine also needs to be a bigger, more welcoming place for populations that have historically not been part of the wine conversation, for people who haven’t historically seen many people who look like them engaging with and enjoying wine.

These, I believe, are the glimmers of promise that can be seen amidst the strobes and heard amongst the thumping bass beats of Vin et Hip-Hop. Whether Vin et Hip-Hop can hold onto that promise while retaining its founding ethos (come in your jeans, come as you are) is the harder trick, and the one worth watching (or listening) for.

The next Vin et Hip-Hop event will take place on October 14th, 2026 at the Château du Clos de Vougeot in Burgundy. Tickets went on sale today, September 16th at 5 PM Central European Time, and were sold out almost instantly, as 5300 people attempted to register simultaneously.

The Hatues Côtes team is already working on Vin et Hip Hop for 2027, with events planned in New York and Los Angeles in March, Champagne in June, and another Burgundy event in October. Bordeaux is purportedly in the works too.

summary:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking

The post Vinography Unboxed: Week of 9/6/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This week I received a couple of wines from Shared Notes Wines, the Sauvignon Blanc-focused project by the wife-and-husband winemaking team of Bibiana Gonzalez Rave and Jeff Pisoni. I’m reviewing both of the wines they make under that brand this week, and both are excellent, with the caveat that their packaging in big, heavy bottles is effectively a big middle finger to the environment. There’s just no reason to package wines like this in bottles that literally weigh more than the wine they contain. Jeff and Bibiana should know better. OK, off of my soapbox, I think I prefer the straight Sauvignon Blanc to their blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon, at least in the 2025 vintage. I love that both are harvested to result in lean, snappy wines that still have some herbaceous qualities in addition to their sunny fruit. Not everyone will be on board with paying nearly $100 for a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, but those who are will find these wines enjoyable.

Chateau Montelena sent through their Sauvignon Blanc as well, and it seemed rather subdued in comparison to the Shared Notes wines, though it is also half the price.

This week I’m reviewing the Cuvée Esme Ann Chenin Blanc from Las Jaras Wines, which is one of my favorite California Chenins for its reductive, snappy, mouthwatering qualities. The fruit comes from the Junius Vineyard (formerly known as Norgard) in Mendocino County and is barrel-fermented and aged in oak, followed by 9 months in stainless steel.

This week I’m also reviewing another batch of wines from Geographic Wines, a project based in Portugal focused on making wines from many of the country’s different wine regions. This week I enjoyed their white blend from old vines in the Douro as well as their old vine red blend of more than 45 grape varieties from the same place. Sadly, these wines aren’t well distributed outside of Europe, so no buying links to offer to my readers for these. Also, the brand’s website is broken, so I can’t even give you somewhere to learn more about them.

I’ve got a couple of old-vine Zinfandels to recommend this week, from Limerick Lane Cellars, whose Marquis Zinfandel comes from a number of storied old-vine Zinfandel vineyards around Sonoma County and has a tremendous juicy lift with little trace of its substantial alcohol levels.

The 2023 Ridge Lytton Springs is a perennial favorite of mine for its complexity, impressive ageworthiness, and just generally mouthwatering offering of blue and black fruits. The 2023 vintage is an impressive edition of this wine that will likely be great for decades.

Speaking of the 2023 vintage, it also did good things for Tierra Roja wines in Napa’s Oakville AVA, where proprietor Linda Neal farms just over 4 acres of Cabernet Sauvignon. Neal worked as a vineyard manager for others in Napa for many years before deciding to focus exclusively on her own property. She makes just a single wine from the plot each year, and the 2023 vintage is certainly one of the best that winemaker Benoit Touquette has made for her.

The name Giacomo Borgogno is well known in Italy’s Piedmont region for having made Barolo since 1761, making it the oldest continuously operating producer in the region. As in many European countries, Italian wines are subject to tasting panels before they are approved to carry the Barolo DOCG designation. In 2005, Borgogno submitted two cask samples to the tasting commission, and one was rejected for not seeming typical in color, despite being made exactly the same as the one that had been accepted. In protest, Borgogno declassified the wine, and No Name Langhe Nebbiolo was born, bearing the designation “a protest label” against appellation bureaucracy. Since then, the Borgogno family has continued to deliberately declassify a portion of their Barolo production each year to make the wine. It is always excellent.

Notes on all these below.

Tasting Notes

2025 Shared Notes “Les Leçons des Maîtres” White Blend, Russian River Valley, Sonoma, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass—nearly colorless—this wine smells of passionfruit, green bell peppers, and honeysuckle. In the mouth, silky, salty flavors of chopped green herbs, green apple skin, and gooseberries have a nice brightness thanks to excellent acidity. A blend of 75% Sauvignon Blanc and 25% Semillon. 13.5% alcohol. 266 cases made. Comes in an unnecessarily heavy bottle weighing 1.54 kg when full. Score: around 9. Cost: $95. click to buy.

2025 Shared Notes “Les Pierres Qui Décident” Sauvignon Blanc, North Coast, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of green apple, passionfruit, cut grass, and a hint of green bell peppers. In the mouth, candied green apple, passionfruit, and gooseberry flavors are electrically bright with excellent acidity and shot through with a hint of crushed nuts and alfalfa. Bright and juicy. A blend of fruit from Sonoma County (70%) and Napa County (30%). 12.87% alcohol. Comes in a nasty, heavy bottle weighing 1.63 kg when full. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $95. click to buy.

2025 Chateau Montelena Sauvignon Blanc, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Palest greenish gold in color, this wine smells of lime zest, green apples, and white flowers. In the mouth, green apple and kiwi notes have a faint grassy quality to them, as well as decent acidity. 14.2% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2023 Las Jaras “Cuvée Esme Anne” Chenin Blanc, Mendocino County, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of struck match, Asian pear, honeysuckle, and candied ginger. In the mouth, candied ginger, Asian pear, struck match, and wet pavement flavors are saline and bright with juicy acidity. Lean and bright, with lovely persistence. Barrel-fermented and aged in oak, followed by 9 months in stainless steel. Bottled unfiltered. 13% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $68.

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Vinhas Velhas Chão de Areia” Vinho Branco, Douro, Portugal
Pale yellow-gold in color, this wine smells of yellow plum, nectarine, and struck flint. In the mouth, salty flavors of unripe nectarines, pomelo zest, saffron, and dried herbs are bright and juicy with a hint of oaky nuttiness. Excellent acidity. A field blend of Rabigato, Viosinho, Gouveio, Códega de Larinho, Síria, and Folgasão. 12% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: ??

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Canais” Touriga Nacional, Douro, Portugal
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black tea, black cherries, crushed peppercorns, and dried herbs. In the mouth, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of black cherries, black tea, and dried herbs. Very good acidity. The tannins gain weight and stiffness with time. 12.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $??

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Vinhas Velhas Almendra” Red Blend, Douro, Portugal
Medium to dark garnet in color, this wine smells of black cherries, black plum, bergamot, earth, and dried flowers. In the mouth, smooth, suede-like tannins coat the mouth and surround a core of black cherries, black plum, currants, dried herbs, and wildflowers. Excellent acidity, lovely balance, and poise. Comes from a field blend of more than 45 different varieties planted in 1850. 12.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $??

2023 Ridge Vineyards “Lytton Springs” Red Blend, Dry Creek Valley, Sonoma, California
Dark purple in the glass, this wine smells of blackberries, black pepper, boysenberries, and cocoa powder. In the mouth, blackberry pie and cocoa powder flavors are wrapped in powdery, mouth-coating tannins that linger with licorice, dried herbs, and sandalwood in the finish. Excellent acidity and balance. 14.4% alcohol. A blend of 76% Zinfandel, 14% Petite Sirah, 7% Carignan, 2% Alicante Bouschet, and 1% Mataro. Vineyard planted in 1905. 11,800 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $56. click to buy.

2023 Limerick Lane Cellars “Marquis” Zinfandel, Russian River Valley, Sonoma, California
Very dark garnet in color, this wine smells of blackberries, licorice, and flowers. In the mouth, juicy floral flavors of boysenberries, raspberries, and orange peel are wrapped in supple, athletic tannins. Great acidity. 15.1% alcohol. 350 cases made. Score: around 9. Cost: $69. click to buy.

2023 Giacomo Borgogno “No Name” Nebbiolo, Langhe, Piedmont, Italy
Light to medium ruby in color with a hint of orange at the rim, this wine smells of strawberries, molasses, and dried flowers. In the mouth, fleecy tannins coat the mouth and stiffen slightly as flavors of strawberries, orange peel, dried herbs, and dried flowers move across the palate. Excellent bright acidity keeps things fresh, and the tannins remain supple and smooth. 14% alcohol. Comes in an unnecessarily heavy bottle weighing 1.53 kg when full. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $51. click to buy.

2023 Tierra Roja Cabernet Sauvignon, Oakville, Napa, California
Inky dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherries, licorice, and cola. In the mouth, juicy black cherries, cola, licorice, and chocolate-covered espresso beans are all wrapped in fleecy tannins. Excellent acidity keeps the wine from feeling too heavy and ripe, though it is quite rich, with sweet oak lingering in the finish. Barrel-fermented in 75% new French oak and then aged for 20 months. 250 cases made. 14.8% alcohol. Comes in a nasty, heavy bottle weighing 1.63 kg when full. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $215. click to buy.
